Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What is the primary aim of accounting according to Chapter 9?
Option A: To determine tax liability exclusively for filing returns with the government
Option B: To maintain secret records of confidential proprietor transactions
Option C: Assessment of business performance for the benefit of all stakeholders
Option D: To physically verify and count goods stored in warehouse godowns
Hint: Consider the foundational definition of accounting given at the start of Section 9.1.
Explanation: According to Section 9.1, the primary aim of accounting is the assessment of business performance for the benefit of all stakeholders (such as owners, employees, suppliers, customers, and financiers) to help them form opinions on financial position.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Final Accounts are best described as financial statements that:
Option A: Validate and explain working results and financial status for a specific period on a particular date
Option B: Record daily cash inflows and outflows on an ongoing chronological basis
Option C: List the personal assets and personal household expenses of the business owner
Option D: Summarize non-monetary agreements and employee performance ratings
Hint: Focus on the definition explaining working results and financial status at the end of a financial year.
Explanation: Final Accounts are financial statements prepared at the end of every financial year that validate and explain the working results and financial status of the business for a specific period on a particular date.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: The balancing figure of a Trading Account represents which of the following?
Option A: Net Profit or Net Loss
Option B: Gross Profit or Gross Loss
Option C: Operating Cash Flow
Option D: Net Capital Employed
Hint: Recall the direct outcome of summarizing trading activities and direct expenses.
Explanation: The balancing figure of the Trading Account is Gross Profit (when credit exceeds debit) or Gross Loss (when debit exceeds credit). Net Profit/Loss is the balancing figure of the Profit and Loss Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: The balancing figure of the Profit and Loss Account reveals:
Option A: Net Profit or Net Loss
Option B: Gross Profit or Gross Loss
Option C: Total Outstanding Liabilities
Option D: Net Purchases for the year
Hint: This final figure accounts for all indirect incomes and indirect expenses.
Explanation: Section 9.1 specifies that in the case of the Profit and Loss Account, the balancing figure is Net Profit or Net Loss, which is ultimately transferred to the Capital Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What is the primary function of a Balance Sheet in Final Accounts?
Option A: To show the financial position of assets and liabilities at a given period of time
Option B: To calculate the gross trading margin earned during the accounting year
Option C: To list all nominal ledger accounts closed during the period
Option D: To record daily sales transactions in chronological sequence
Hint: The Balance Sheet is a positional statement rather than an operating account.
Explanation: The Balance Sheet is a statement showing the true financial position of assets and liabilities of a business concern on a specified date.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of preparing Final Accounts as listed in the chapter?
Option A: To determine Gross Profit/Gross Loss and Net Profit/Net Loss during the financial year
Option B: To show the true and correct financial position of the business
Option C: To enable effective control over the financial activities of the business
Option D: To eliminate the necessity of recording primary transactions in journals
Hint: Final accounts depend on journal entries rather than replacing them.
Explanation: The stated objectives include determining profit/loss, showing true financial position, informing stakeholders, and controlling financial activities. Eliminating primary journal books is incorrect because Final Accounts are drafted from ledger balances originating from journals.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Final Accounts are important for tax compliance because they help provide a clear break-up of amounts payable to the government for:
Option A: Customs penalties only
Option B: Proprietor's personal residential property taxes
Option C: Foreign trade tariffs on domestic production
Option D: Various taxes like Income Tax and GST
Hint: Look under Section 9.1(C) for specific examples of statutory taxes mentioned.
Explanation: Section 9.1(C) states that Final Accounts help obtain a clear break-up of amounts payable to the government as various taxes, such as Income Tax and GST.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which chronological sequence correctly depicts the accounting process ending in Final Accounts?
Option A: Business Transactions -> Trial Balance -> Ledger Posting -> Journal Entries -> Final Accounts
Option B: Journal Entries -> Business Transactions -> Balancing the ledger -> Trial Balance -> Final Accounts
Option C: Trial Balance -> Balancing the ledger -> Ledger Posting -> Business Transactions -> Final Accounts
Option D: Business Transactions -> Journal Entries -> Ledger Posting -> Balancing the ledger -> Trial Balance -> Final Accounts
Hint: Trace the step-by-step workflow chart shown on page 273.
Explanation: Page 273 illustrates the accounting process as: Business Transactions -> Journal Entries -> Ledger Posting -> Balancing the ledger -> Trial Balance -> Final Accounts at the end of every year.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: According to the syllabus note in Chapter 9, which components are specifically included in Final Accounts for XI Commerce?
Option A: Manufacturing Account and Profit & Loss Appropriation Account only
Option B: Trading Account and Manufacturing Account only
Option C: Trading Account, Profit and Loss Account, and Balance Sheet
Option D: Cash Flow Statement and Profit & Loss Appropriation Account
Hint: Check the syllabus note explicitly mentioning what is included and excluded for XI Commerce.
Explanation: A syllabus note on page 273 explains that Manufacturing Account and Profit & Loss Appropriation Account are not included in the XI Commerce syllabus; Final Accounts consist only of Trading Account, Profit and Loss Account, and Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Trading Account is classified under which type of account?
Option A: Real Account
Option B: Personal Account
Option C: Nominal Account
Option D: Representative Personal Account
Hint: It deals with revenues, expenses, purchases, and direct costs.
Explanation: Page 273 explicitly states: 'Trading Account is a Nominal Account.' It records expenses and losses on the debit side and revenues/goods movements on the credit side.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which of the following items is credited to the Trading Account?
Option A: Goods distributed as free sample
Option B: Freight and Carriage Inward
Option C: Custom Duty
Option D: Motive Power and Fuel
Hint: Think of items representing outward movements or deductions of goods from business stock.
Explanation: Outward movements of goods such as sales, goods distributed as free samples, goods withdrawn by proprietor for personal use, and closing stock are credited to the Trading Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: In trading terminology, unsold goods at the beginning of an accounting year are called:
Option A: Closing Stock
Option B: Reserve Stock
Option C: Dead Stock
Option D: Opening Stock
Hint: This refers to the unsold goods carried forward from the preceding period.
Explanation: Under important terms of Trading Account (page 274), goods that are unsold are called Stock, and unsold goods at the beginning of the year are specifically referred to as Opening Stock.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Closing Stock is always valued in the Final Accounts at:
Option A: Market price only
Option B: Cost price only
Option C: Cost or market price, whichever is more
Option D: Cost or market price, whichever is less
Hint: This is rooted in the accounting convention of conservatism/prudence.
Explanation: Section 9.2 states that closing stock is always valued at cost or market price, whichever is less (conservatism principle).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: If closing stock is valued at Cost Price ₹46,000 and Market Price ₹40,000, what amount will appear in the Trading Account and Balance Sheet?
Hint: Apply the rule: cost price or market price, whichever is less.
Explanation: Closing stock is valued at cost or market price, whichever is less. Between ₹46,000 and ₹40,000, the lower figure is ₹40,000 (as illustrated in Illustration 3).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which of the following transactions must be debited to Purchases Account and included in the Trading Account?
Option A: Purchase of office furniture for business use
Option B: Purchase of plant and machinery on credit
Option C: Purchase of merchandise/goods meant for resale
Option D: Purchase of government debentures as an investment
Hint: Purchases in Trading Account includes only goods, not capital assets.
Explanation: Page 274 states: 'Purchases: This includes the purchases of goods and not purchases of assets.' Fixed asset acquisitions are capitalized to their respective asset accounts.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Return Outwards is another accounting name for:
Option A: Sales Returns
Option B: Purchase Returns
Option C: Goods returned by customers
Option D: Drawings of goods by proprietor
Hint: These are goods sent out back to suppliers.
Explanation: Purchase Returns are also called Return Outwards. They are deducted from total purchases to record net purchases on the debit side of the Trading Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: How are Return Inwards treated in the preparation of the Trading Account?
Option A: Added to Purchases on the debit side
Option B: Shown as an asset in the Balance Sheet
Option C: Deducted from gross Sales on the credit side
Option D: Debited to Profit and Loss Account as an indirect loss
Hint: Return Inward represents goods coming back in from buyers.
Explanation: Return Inwards (Sales Returns) are deducted from gross sales on the credit side of the Trading Account to determine net sales.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Direct expenses in final accounts are defined as expenses incurred for:
Option A: Office management and executive staff salaries
Option B: Selling and advertising goods across regional markets
Option C: Purchase of goods, production of goods, and purchase expenses
Option D: Financing bank loans and servicing interest
Hint: Think of expenses directly tied to manufacturing or bringing goods to the trading location.
Explanation: Direct expenses are defined in Section 9.2 as expenses incurred for the purchase of goods, production of goods, and purchase expenses (e.g., wages, freight inward, coal, gas, dock dues).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Carriage Inward and Carriage Outward are treated respectively in:
Option A: Debit of Profit and Loss Account and Debit of Trading Account
Option B: Credit of Trading Account and Debit of Balance Sheet
Option C: Both debited to Trading Account
Option D: Debit of Trading Account and Debit of Profit and Loss Account
Hint: Inward carriage relates to buying goods, while outward carriage relates to delivering goods sold.
Explanation: Carriage Inward is a direct expense incurred on bringing goods purchased to the business premises (debited to Trading A/c). Carriage Outward is a selling and distribution expense (debited to Profit and Loss A/c).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: When an item appears as 'Wages & Salaries' in the Trial Balance, where should it be debited?
Option A: Profit & Loss Account
Option B: Trading Account
Option C: Balance Sheet under Assets
Option D: Directly deducted from Capital
Hint: The first named term dictates the primary nature of the composite expense.
Explanation: When 'Wages' appears first (i.e., 'Wages & Salaries'), it is treated as a productive/direct factory expense and debited to the Trading Account. If 'Salaries & Wages' appears, it is debited to the Profit & Loss Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: In practical final accounts, Productive Wages and Unproductive Wages are debited respectively to:
Option A: Profit and Loss Account and Trading Account
Option B: Trading Account and Profit and Loss Account
Option C: Both to Trading Account
Option D: Both to Profit and Loss Account
Hint: Productive wages are linked to factory production, while unproductive wages relate to general/administrative operations.
Explanation: As seen in practical problem 6, Productive Wages are directly tied to manufacturing and debited to Trading A/c, whereas Unproductive Wages are indirect operational costs debited to Profit & Loss A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What is the correct journal entry to close Opening Stock, Purchases, and Direct Expenses to the Trading Account?
Option A: Opening Stock A/c Dr., Purchases A/c Dr., Direct Expenses A/c Dr. To Trading A/c
Option B: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Trading A/c
Option C: Trading A/c Dr. To Opening Stock A/c, To Purchases A/c, To Direct Expenses A/c
Option D: Trading A/c Dr. To Capital A/c
Hint: Trading Account is debited to close debit balances of direct expense and stock accounts.
Explanation: Section 9.2 gives the closing entry: Trading A/c Dr. To Opening Stock A/c, To Direct Expenses A/c, To Purchases A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which journal entry is passed to transfer Sales to the Trading Account at the end of the year?
Option A: Trading A/c Dr. To Sales A/c
Option B: Sales A/c Dr. To Profit & Loss A/c
Option C: Sales A/c Dr. To Trading A/c
Option D: Sales A/c Dr. To Sundry Debtors A/c
Hint: Sales Account has a credit balance, so it is debited to close and transfer it.
Explanation: To transfer the credit balance of Sales Account to Trading Account, the entry is: Sales A/c Dr. To Trading A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: When the Trading Account reveals a Gross Profit, which closing entry is passed?
Option A: Trading A/c Dr. To Profit & Loss A/c
Option B: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Trading A/c
Option C: Capital A/c Dr. To Trading A/c
Option D: Trading A/c Dr. To Capital A/c
Hint: Gross profit is transferred from the debit side of Trading A/c to the credit of Profit & Loss A/c.
Explanation: Gross Profit represents a credit excess in Trading A/c. To transfer it to P&L A/c, Trading A/c is debited and Profit & Loss A/c is credited: Trading A/c Dr. To Profit & Loss A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Given: Opening Stock ₹5,000, Purchases ₹15,500, Purchases Returns ₹500, Carriage Inward ₹1,200, Sales ₹30,000, Closing Stock ₹18,000. What is the Gross Profit?
Hint: Calculate Credit side total (Sales + Closing Stock) and subtract Debit side total (Opening Stock + Net Purchases + Carriage Inward).
Explanation: Credit side = Sales (₹30,000) + Closing Stock (₹18,000) = ₹48,000. Debit side = Opening Stock (₹5,000) + Net Purchases (₹15,500 - ₹500 = ₹15,000) + Carriage Inward (₹1,200) = ₹21,200. Gross Profit = ₹48,000 - ₹21,200 = ₹26,800.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What type of account is the Profit and Loss Account, and what does it ascertain?
Option A: Personal Account; ascertains proprietor's personal net worth
Option B: Real Account; ascertains the market value of tangible assets
Option C: Valuation Account; ascertains accumulated depreciation
Option D: Nominal Account; ascertains Net Profit or Net Loss
Hint: It records indirect expenses/losses and revenues/gains.
Explanation: Page 276 states: 'Profit and Loss Account is a Nominal Account' maintained to ascertain Net Profit or Net Loss, providing the final working results of the business.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which group consists exclusively of expenses debited to the Profit and Loss Account?
Option A: Wages, Freight Inward, Royalties, Custom Duty
Option B: Opening Stock, Purchases, Motive Power, Factory Lighting
Option C: Bills Payable, Creditors, Bank Loan, Capital
Option D: Salaries, Audit Fees, Advertisement, Printing & Stationery
Hint: Look for office, administrative, and selling expenses rather than factory costs or liabilities.
Explanation: Salaries, audit fees, advertisement, and printing & stationery are indirect administrative and selling expenses debited to Profit and Loss Account. The items in A and C are direct expenses debited to Trading Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: When the credit side of the Profit and Loss Account exceeds its debit side, the resulting balance is:
Option A: Gross Profit
Option B: Net Loss
Option C: Net Profit
Option D: Gross Loss
Hint: Credit side reflects indirect revenues/gains, while debit side reflects indirect expenses/losses.
Explanation: When total credit (incomes) exceeds total debit (expenses) in the Profit and Loss Account, the excess is Net Profit. An excess of debit over credit is Net Loss.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which journal entry is passed to transfer Net Profit to the proprietor's Capital Account?
Option A: Capital A/c Dr. To Profit & Loss A/c
Option B: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Capital A/c
Option C: Trading A/c Dr. To Capital A/c
Option D: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Drawings A/c
Hint: Net Profit increases the proprietor's capital, meaning Capital Account must be credited.
Explanation: Net Profit is transferred by debiting Profit & Loss Account and crediting Capital Account: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Capital A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What is the journal entry for transferring a Net Loss to the Capital Account?
Option A: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Capital A/c
Option B: Net Loss A/c Dr. To Trading A/c
Option C: Balance Sheet A/c Dr. To Capital A/c
Option D: Capital A/c Dr. To Profit & Loss A/c
Hint: Net Loss reduces capital, so the Capital Account must be debited.
Explanation: A net loss reduces proprietor's equity. The transfer entry is: Capital A/c Dr. To Profit & Loss A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Why does a Balance Sheet NOT have 'To' or 'By' written against its items?
Option A: Because it is an informal estimation of assets
Option B: Because it is a statement of financial position and not a ledger account
Option C: Because it records only cash transactions
Option D: Because it only contains credit balances of personal accounts
Hint: Note the distinction between an account and a statement.
Explanation: Section 9.4 explains that the Balance Sheet has no debit or credit side because it is a statement and not an account. Hence, words like 'To' and 'By' are not used.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which category of accounts NEVER appears in the Balance Sheet?
Option A: Nominal Accounts
Option B: Real Accounts
Option C: Personal Accounts
Option D: Tangible Asset Accounts
Hint: These accounts represent revenues and expenses and are already closed into Trading and P&L Accounts.
Explanation: Page 280 explicitly notes: 'No Nominal Account will appear in the Balance Sheet.' All nominal accounts are closed to Trading A/c or Profit & Loss A/c. Only Personal and Real accounts appear in the Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: In a Balance Sheet, debit balances and credit balances are recorded respectively on the:
Option A: Liability side (left) and Asset side (right)
Option B: Asset side (right) and Liability side (left)
Option C: Debit side (left) and Credit side (right)
Option D: Asset side (left) and Liability side (right)
Hint: Personal/real debit balances are assets (right hand side), credit balances are liabilities (left hand side).
Explanation: Debit balances of Personal and Real accounts appear on the Asset side (right-hand side), while credit balances of Personal accounts appear on the Liability side (left-hand side).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What is the primary difference in treatment between an item given in the Trial Balance and an item given in the Adjustments?
Option A: Trial Balance items have at least two effects, while adjustments have only one effect
Option B: Trial Balance items have only one effect, while every adjustment has at least two effects
Option C: Trial Balance items are debited to Balance Sheet, while adjustments are credited to Trading A/c
Option D: Both Trial Balance items and adjustments must always have three effects
Hint: Recall the True/False section and general rule regarding double-entry bookkeeping for unrecorded information.
Explanation: Every item in the Trial Balance has already completed its double entry and receives only one effect in Final Accounts, whereas every adjustment represents an unrecorded item requiring at least two effects.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Depreciation is defined in Chapter 9 as:
Option A: Sudden accidental destruction of goods by fire or natural calamity
Option B: Failure of credit debtors to pay their overdue accounts
Option C: Gradual and continuous decrease or reduction in the value of fixed assets
Option D: A cash allowance granted to customers for prompt settlement
Hint: Review the definition under Section 9.5, item 2.
Explanation: Section 9.5 defines depreciation as: 'gradual and continuous decrease or reduction in the value of assets. This amount of depreciation is charged on fixed assets.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What are the two accounting effects of depreciation provided on fixed assets in Final Accounts?
Option A: Debited to Trading Account and added to Asset in Balance Sheet
Option B: Debited to Profit & Loss Account and deducted from respective Asset in Balance Sheet
Option C: Credited to Profit & Loss Account and added to Liabilities in Balance Sheet
Option D: Debited to Capital Account and credited to Trading Account
Hint: Depreciation is a non-cash business loss that lowers the book value of the asset.
Explanation: Depreciation is debited to the Profit & Loss Account (as an indirect operating loss/expense) and deducted from the respective asset on the Asset side of the Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Machinery of ₹35,500 is purchased on 1st July 2018, and ₹4,500 is spent on its installation on the same day. What is the depreciation at 7% p.a. for the accounting year ending 31st March 2019 (9 months)?
Hint: Add installation expenses to the purchase cost to get total capital cost, then calculate 7% for 9/12 of the year.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Plant & Machinery balance is ₹1,80,000, which includes ₹40,000 for new machinery purchased on 1st October. If depreciation is 10% p.a. and year ends on 31st March, total depreciation is:
Hint: Depreciate the old machinery (₹1,40,000) for full 12 months and new machinery (₹40,000) for 6 months.
Explanation: Old machinery = ₹1,80,000 - ₹40,000 = ₹1,40,000; 10% for full year = ₹14,000. New machinery = ₹40,000; 10% for 6 months = ₹2,000. Total depreciation = ₹14,000 + ₹2,000 = ₹16,000 (Illustration 9).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Expenses incurred during the current accounting year but not yet paid are known as:
Option A: Prepaid Expenses
Option B: Accrued Incomes
Option C: Outstanding Expenses
Option D: Deferred Revenue Incomes
Hint: They represent unpaid obligations for benefits already consumed.
Explanation: Section 9.5 defines Outstanding expenses as: 'The expenses which have been incurred but not paid during the year are unpaid expenses.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What are the two accounting effects of Outstanding Expenses given in adjustments?
Option A: Deducted from the respective expense in Trading/P&L Account and shown on the Asset side
Option B: Credited to Trading Account and debited to Capital Account
Option C: Debited to Balance Sheet and credited to Cash Account
Option D: Added to the respective expense in Trading/P&L Account and shown on the Liability side of the Balance Sheet
Hint: They increase the current year's expense and represent a pending obligation.
Explanation: Outstanding expenses are added to the particular expense on the Trading or Profit & Loss Account and shown on the Liability side of the Balance Sheet as a current liability.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Expenses paid during the current year in advance for the subsequent period are termed:
Option A: Prepaid (Unexpired) Expenses
Option B: Outstanding Expenses
Option C: Accrued Income
Option D: Capital Expenditure
Hint: These are expenses whose economic benefit extends beyond the balance sheet date.
Explanation: Under Section 9.5, expenses paid in advance of the current year are defined as Prepaid expenses or Unexpired expenses.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: How are Prepaid Expenses treated in Final Accounts?
Option A: Added to respective expense in Trading/P&L A/c and shown on Liability side
Option B: Credited to P&L A/c and deducted from Capital
Option C: Deducted from respective expense in Trading/P&L A/c and shown on Asset side of Balance Sheet
Option D: Debited to Trading A/c and credited to Cash A/c
Hint: They reduce current year expenses and represent future service/benefits owned.
Explanation: Prepaid expenses are deducted from the respective expense on the debit side of the Trading or Profit & Loss Account and shown on the Asset side of the Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: An annual insurance premium of ₹8,000 is paid on 1st December 2018. For the accounting year ending 31st March 2019, how much insurance is prepaid?
Hint: The policy runs for 12 months up to 30th November 2019. Determine how many months fall after 31st March 2019.
Explanation: The premium covers 12 months (1st Dec 2018 to 30th Nov 2019). The current year uses 4 months (Dec to March = ₹8,000 * 4/12 = ₹2,667). The prepaid portion is for the remaining 8 months: ₹8,000 * 8/12 = ₹5,333.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Income earned during the accounting year but not yet received by the year-end is classified as:
Option A: Pre-received Income
Option B: Accrued Income (Outstanding Income)
Option C: Unearned Revenue
Option D: Contingent Asset
Hint: The earning process is complete, but cash settlement remains pending.
Explanation: Section 9.5 defines Accrued Income (or Outstanding Income) as income that has been earned during the accounting year but not yet received.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What are the two effects of Accrued Income in Final Accounts?
Option A: Deducted from income in P&L A/c and shown on Liability side
Option B: Added to sales in Trading A/c and added to Debtors
Option C: Added to particular income on credit side of P&L A/c and shown on Asset side of Balance Sheet
Option D: Debited to P&L A/c and deducted from Capital
Hint: It represents earned revenue for the year and an asset receivable.
Explanation: Accrued income is added to the respective income on the credit side of Profit & Loss Account and shown on the Asset side of the Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: How is income received in advance (relating to the next accounting period) treated in Final Accounts?
Option A: Deducted from particular income on credit side of P&L A/c and shown on Liability side of Balance Sheet
Option B: Added to income in P&L A/c and shown on Asset side
Option C: Debited to Trading A/c and shown on Asset side
Option D: Credited to Trading A/c and deducted from Creditors
Hint: It does not belong to the current year's earnings and creates an obligation/liability.
Explanation: Income received in advance is deducted from the respective income on the credit side of Profit & Loss Account and shown as a liability on the Liability side of the Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: In accounting, debts that are irrecoverable from customers are called:
Option A: Bad Debts
Option B: Doubtful Debts
Option C: Trade Discounts
Option D: Cash Discounts
Hint: Recovery of this amount is completely ruled out.
Explanation: Page 281 states: 'The Debts which are irrecoverable is called Bad-debts. The amount of Bad debts is loss to business.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What journal entry is passed when Bad Debts are written off from debtors?
Option A: Sundry Debtors A/c Dr. To Bad Debts A/c
Option B: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Cash A/c
Option C: Bad Debts A/c Dr. To Capital A/c
Option D: Bad Debts A/c Dr. To Sundry Debtors A/c
Hint: Bad Debts is a loss (debited) and reduces debtors (credited).
Explanation: When bad debts are written off, the entry is: Bad Debts A/c Dr. To Sundry Debtors A/c. Subsequently, Bad Debts is transferred to Profit & Loss A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Why is a Reserve for Doubtful Debts (R.D.D.) created in final accounts?
Option A: To record debts that are already settled and received in cash
Option B: To provide for anticipated loss on debtors whose recovery is doubtful based on past experience
Option C: To offer prompt cash settlement bonuses to suppliers
Option D: To comply with mandatory company dividend reserve regulations
Hint: It addresses potential, expected non-realization rather than established bad debts.
Explanation: Section 9.5 states that recovery of some debtors is doubtful. Based on previous years' experience, a provision is created for this anticipated loss, known as Reserve for Doubtful Debts.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: According to the chapter notes, R.D.D. appearing in the Trial Balance is referred to as:
Option A: New R.D.D.
Option B: Contingent Reserve
Option C: General Reserve
Option D: Old R.D.D. (Existing R.D.D.)
Hint: Check Note 2 under Section 9.5 on page 282.
Explanation: Note 2 on page 282 explicitly states: 'When R.D.D. is given in Trial Balance, it is known as old R.D.D. [Existing R.D.D.]. When R.D.D. is given in adjustment, it is called New R.D.D.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: When New Bad Debts, New R.D.D., and Provision for Discount on Debtors are all given in adjustments, in what order must they be computed?
Option A: Discount on Debtors first, then R.D.D., then Bad Debts
Option B: New R.D.D. first, then Bad Debts, then Discount on Debtors
Option C: All three calculated simultaneously on gross Sundry Debtors
Option D: New Bad Debts first, then New R.D.D. on the remaining balance, then Provision for Discount on Debtors on the net balance
Hint: You must deduct actual uncollectible amounts first, provide for doubtful debts second, and discount only good debtors.
Explanation: Page 282 notes that Provision for Discount on Debtors is calculated after deducting New Bad Debts and New R.D.D. First deduct New Bad Debts from Sundry Debtors, compute New R.D.D. on the balance, and finally compute discount on the remaining good balance.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Sundry Debtors in Trial Balance is ₹20,250. Adjustments specify: Write off ₹1,000 as bad debts, provide 2% R.D.D. on debtors, and provide 3% discount on creditors (Creditors = ₹18,500). What is the New R.D.D. amount?
Hint: Deduct bad debts (₹1,000) from Debtors (₹20,250) before applying the 2% rate.
Explanation: Debtors after bad debts = ₹20,250 - ₹1,000 = ₹19,250. New R.D.D. = 2% of ₹19,250 = ₹385 (Working Note, Illustration 4). ₹555 is discount on creditors.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Which adjustment is specifically identified in Chapter 9 as the 'only exception to the convention of conservatism'?
Option A: Reserve for Doubtful Debts
Option B: Provision for Discount on Creditors
Option C: Depreciation on fixed assets
Option D: Valuing closing stock at cost or market price whichever is less
Hint: This provision anticipates a prospective gain/profit from suppliers before it is actually realized.
Explanation: Page 282 explicitly states: 'Provision/Reserve for Discount on Creditors: ...discount received from creditors is treated as Profit or gain. So it is to be credited to Profit & Loss A/c and to be deducted from creditors from Balance Sheet. It is the only exception to the convention of conservatism.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What are the two accounting effects of creating a Provision for Discount on Creditors?
Option A: Debited to P&L A/c and added to Creditors in Balance Sheet
Option B: Credited to Trading Account and deducted from Debtors
Option C: Credited to Profit & Loss Account and deducted from Sundry Creditors in Balance Sheet
Option D: Debited to Capital Account and added to Bills Payable
Hint: It is treated as an expected gain and reduces the payable amount.
Explanation: Section 9.5 (Adjustment 10) provides that Provision for Discount on Creditors is credited to the Profit & Loss Account and deducted from Sundry Creditors on the Liabilities side of the Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: If Old R.D.D. in Trial Balance is ₹2,500, New Bad Debts is ₹0, Old Bad Debts is ₹600, and New R.D.D. is ₹1,500, where and how is the excess ₹400 shown?
Option A: Debited to Profit & Loss Account
Option B: Deducted from Capital on the Liability side
Option C: Credited to Profit & Loss Account as a gain
Option D: Added to Sundry Debtors in the Balance Sheet
Hint: When existing provision exceeds required provision plus bad debts, the surplus is a gain.
Explanation: As demonstrated in Illustration 12 Working Note: Old R.D.D. (₹2,500) > [New R.D.D. (₹1,500) + Bad Debts (₹600) = ₹2,100]. The excess provision of ₹400 is credited to Profit and Loss Account as a gain.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What are the two accounting effects when goods are withdrawn by the proprietor for personal use?
Option A: Debited to Trading A/c and credited to Cash A/c
Option B: Debited to P&L A/c and added to Debtors in Balance Sheet
Option C: Credited to Trading A/c (or deducted from purchases) and deducted from Capital on the Liability side
Option D: Credited to Sales A/c and added to Capital on the Liability side
Hint: Goods leave the business without generating sales, and proprietor's investment decreases.
Explanation: Goods withdrawn for personal use reduce the cost of trading inventory (credited to Trading A/c or deducted from Purchases) and are treated as drawings (deducted from Capital on the Liability side).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Distribution of goods as a free sample is an advertisement. What are its two accounting effects?
Option A: Debited to Trading A/c and added to Debtors in Balance Sheet
Option B: Credited to Trading A/c (or deducted from purchases) and debited to Profit & Loss Account under Advertisement
Option C: Credited to Profit & Loss Account and deducted from Creditors
Option D: Debited to Capital Account and credited to Sales A/c
Hint: It reduces goods available for sale and represents an advertising expense.
Explanation: Section 9.5 (Adjustment 12) explains that goods given as free samples reduce merchandise stock (credited to Trading A/c or deducted from purchases) and are debited to Profit & Loss Account as Advertisement expense.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Interest allowed on Capital is treated in Final Accounts as:
Option A: Credited to Profit & Loss Account and deducted from Capital
Option B: Debited to Trading Account and added to Cash at Bank
Option C: Debited to Capital and credited to Drawings
Option D: Debited to Profit & Loss Account and added to Capital in Balance Sheet
Hint: From the business's viewpoint, it is an expense paid to the owner, increasing the owner's total capital claim.
Explanation: Interest on capital is an expense to the business concern (debited to Profit & Loss Account) and an addition to the proprietor's investment (added to Capital on the Liability side of the Balance Sheet).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: What are the two effects of Interest on Drawings in Final Accounts?
Option A: Credited to Profit & Loss Account and deducted from Capital (or added to Drawings)
Option B: Debited to P&L A/c and added to Capital
Option C: Debited to Trading A/c and added to Cash in hand
Option D: Credited to Balance Sheet and debited to Bank Loan
Hint: Interest charged on drawings is an income for the business and reduces the owner's equity.
Explanation: Section 9.5 (Adjustment 14) states that Interest on Drawings is credited to the Profit & Loss Account (as an indirect income/gain) and deducted from Capital (or added to Drawings) on the Liability side of the Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: When the specific date of drawings is not mentioned in the Trial Balance or adjustment, interest on drawings is charged for:
Option A: The full twelve months
Option B: Three months only
Option C: An average period of six months
Option D: Nine months
Hint: Recall Question 3(10) of the Chapter Exercises and the note in Illustration 8.
Explanation: The chapter note in Illustration 8 and Exercise Q.3(10) explicitly state: 'When specific date is not given, in that case interest on drawing is charged for 6 months.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Drawings given in Trial Balance is ₹2,500. Rate of interest on drawings is 7% p.a. No date of withdrawal is mentioned. What is the amount of interest on drawings?
Hint: Calculate 7% on ₹2,500 and then take half (6 months).
Explanation: Annual interest = ₹2,500 * (7/100) = ₹175. Since no date is given, interest is charged for 6 months: ₹175 / 2 = ₹87.50, rounded to ₹88 (as shown in Illustration 8).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Given: Building ₹20,000, Furniture ₹15,000, Debtors ₹30,000, Investments ₹10,000, Cash at Bank ₹5,000, Plant & Machinery ₹20,000; Bills Payable ₹18,000, Creditors ₹20,700, Outstanding Wages ₹1,250. What is Capital?
Hint: Total Assets minus Total External Liabilities equals Capital.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: A 6% Bank Loan of ₹50,000 was taken on 1st October 2017. If the accounting year ends on 31st March 2018 and no interest appears in the Trial Balance, what is the outstanding interest on loan?
Hint: Apply 6% p.a. for the 6 months elapsed between October 1 and March 31.
Explanation: Loan was borrowed on 1st October 2017, so interest is chargeable for 6 months (Oct to March). Interest = ₹50,000 * 6% * (6/12) = ₹1,500 (Illustration 6 Working Note).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: In a Trial Balance for the year ending 31st March, Salaries appears as '₹5,000 (for 10 months)'. What is the outstanding salary to be added in Profit & Loss A/c and shown in Balance Sheet?
Hint: Determine monthly salary by dividing ₹5,000 by 10, then find the amount for the remaining 2 months.
Explanation: Monthly salary = ₹5,000 / 10 = ₹500 per month. Outstanding period = 12 - 10 = 2 months. Outstanding amount = 2 * ₹500 = ₹1,000 (Illustration 4 Working Note).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: How is Goodwill classified in the Balance Sheet?
Option A: Current Liability
Option B: Fictitious Asset
Option C: Nominal Loss
Option D: Intangible Fixed Asset (not a fictitious asset)
Hint: Check the True/False question discussing whether goodwill is a fictitious asset.
Explanation: Exercise Q.4(4) confirms that 'Goodwill is not a fictitious asset.' It is an intangible real asset shown on the Asset side of the Balance Sheet.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Bank Overdraft is classified and shown in the Balance Sheet as a/an:
Option A: Current / External Liability
Option B: Internal Liability to the proprietor
Option C: Current Asset
Option D: Contingent Asset
Hint: It is an amount owed to the bank, repayable on demand.
Explanation: Bank Overdraft is a short-term external loan payable to the bank and is shown under Liabilities in the Balance Sheet. Disagreeing with 'Bank Overdraft is an internal liability' is confirmed in Exercise Q.7(4).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Bills Receivable and Bills Payable appear respectively in the Balance Sheet under:
Option A: Liabilities and Assets
Option B: Both under Assets
Option C: Assets and Liabilities
Option D: Both under Liabilities
Hint: Receivables represent claims owned; payables represent claims owed.
Explanation: Bills Receivable is an asset (debt claim due to the business), whereas Bills Payable is a liability (debt owed by the business).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: An advance given to workers appearing as an adjustment (e.g., 'Wages include ₹800 advance to workers') is treated as:
Option A: Deducted from Wages in Trading A/c and shown as an Asset in Balance Sheet
Option B: Added to Wages in Trading A/c and shown on Liability side
Option C: Debited to P&L A/c and credited to Cash
Option D: Credited to Sales A/c and added to Debtors
Hint: Advances are pre-payments, not current expenses, and represent amounts recoverable or adjustable against future work.
Explanation: Advance to workers is prepaid labor cost: it is deducted from Wages in Trading Account and shown on the Asset side of the Balance Sheet (Illustration 11).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: In Final Accounts, Factory Rent and Office Rent are recorded respectively in:
Option A: Trading Account and Profit & Loss Account
Option B: Profit & Loss Account and Trading Account
Option C: Both in Profit & Loss Account
Option D: Both in Trading Account
Hint: Factory expenses relate to manufacturing goods, while office expenses relate to administrative operations.
Explanation: Factory Rent is a direct manufacturing expense debited to Trading Account, whereas Office Rent is an administrative indirect expense debited to Profit & Loss Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: In a Trial Balance containing Trade Expenses, Salaries, and Office Expenses, Trade Expenses should be:
Option A: Debited to Profit & Loss Account
Option B: Credited to Trading Account
Option C: Deducted from Sales
Option D: Capitalized to Machinery
Hint: In the specimen and textbook illustrations (e.g., Illustration 10 and Practical Problem 6), Trade Expenses is treated as an indirect expense.
Explanation: In Chapter 9 illustrations and practical problems (such as Illustration 10 and Practical Problem 6), Trade Expenses is classified as an indirect operating expense and debited to the Profit & Loss Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Motive Power, Fuel, Gas, and Water are recorded in:
Option A: Credit side of Profit and Loss Account
Option B: Debit side of Trading Account
Option C: Asset side of Balance Sheet
Option D: Debit side of Profit and Loss Account
Hint: These are direct factory operating utilities required to run machinery.
Explanation: Motive power, coal, gas, fuel, and water are direct manufacturing expenses debited to the Trading Account (Section 9.2 specimen and Illustration 1).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Royalties paid on production/goods are debited to:
Option A: Profit & Loss Account
Option B: Trading Account
Option C: Balance Sheet under Intangible Assets
Option D: Drawings Account
Hint: Royalties are direct expenses incurred in the acquisition or production of goods.
Explanation: Section 9.2 specimen and Illustration 1 clearly show Royalties debited to the Trading Account as a direct production cost.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Discount received from creditors on prompt payment is an indirect income and is transferred to:
Option A: Credit side of Trading Account
Option B: Credit side of Profit & Loss Account
Option C: Debit side of Profit & Loss Account
Option D: Liability side of Balance Sheet as an addition to creditors
Hint: Incomes and gains are credited to the Profit and Loss Account.
Explanation: Exercise Q.3(2) and Section 9.3 state: 'Discount earned is transferred to credit side of Profit & Loss account' as an indirect revenue/gain.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: Trial Balance shows Salaries ₹18,000 with note: '2/3rd for factory'. What amount of salaries will be debited to Trading Account and Profit & Loss Account respectively?
Option A: ₹12,000 to Trading Account and ₹6,000 to Profit & Loss Account
Option B: ₹18,000 to Trading Account and ₹0 to P&L Account
Option C: ₹6,000 to Trading Account and ₹12,000 to Profit & Loss Account
Option D: ₹9,000 to Trading Account and ₹9,000 to Profit & Loss Account
Hint: Factory portion (2/3) goes to Trading Account as direct expense, and remaining 1/3 goes to P&L Account as indirect expense.
Explanation: Factory salaries = 2/3 of ₹18,000 = ₹12,000 (debited to Trading A/c). The remaining office portion = 1/3 of ₹18,000 = ₹6,000 (debited to Profit & Loss A/c), as seen in Practical Problem 4.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Chapter: Chapter 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
Question: When an item 'Loss by fire ₹1,650' appears directly as a debit balance in the Trial Balance, how is it treated?
Option A: Debited to Profit & Loss Account only
Option B: Debited to Trading Account only
Option C: Credited to Trading Account and shown as Asset in Balance Sheet
Option D: Deducted from Capital and credited to Purchases
Hint: Items inside the Trial Balance have only one effect.
Explanation: Since 'Loss by fire' is already inside the Trial Balance (as in Illustration 8), it represents an established loss and has only ONE effect: it is debited to the Profit and Loss Account.
